planting.note: Set out divisions or container plants in spring in lean, sharply drained soil in full sun; established mats resent standing water and heavy clay.

directions: Woolly Yarrow forms a dense, low mat of soft, gray-green, finely dissected foliage topped in early to midsummer by flat clusters of bright golden-yellow flowers on short stems. It is one of the few true groundcover yarrows, spreading steadily by rhizomes to knit together bare, sunny slopes, gravel gardens, and spaces between paving stones without becoming aggressive in lean soil. Shear off spent flower stalks after bloom to keep the mat tidy and encourage denser regrowth; avoid rich, moist soil or overhead watering in humid climates, which promotes rot and loosens the tight habit. It tolerates poor, rocky, and alkaline soils better than most perennials and needs no fertilizer.

planting.note: Plant in gritty, sharply drained, lean soil in full sun; raised beds, rock gardens, or scree plantings suit it far better than flat, moisture-retentive ground.

directions: Native to mountain screes in the Balkans and Greece, this diminutive yarrow forms a tight, silvery-gray tomentose mat only a few inches tall, studded from late spring into summer with white daisy-like flowers held just above the foliage. It is grown chiefly as a foliage and texture plant for rock gardens, troughs, and gravel paths, where its silver carpet contrasts with bolder-leaved neighbors. Sharp drainage is essential year-round; it is far more likely to be lost to winter wet than winter cold. Shear lightly after flowering to keep the mat compact, and avoid mulching directly over the crown, which encourages rot in humid summers.

common_name: King Edward Yarrow (Compact Primrose-Yellow Rock Garden Yarrow)

planting.note: Set out divisions or container plants in spring in gritty, lean, very well-drained soil in full sun; this hybrid is propagated by division since it does not come true from seed.

directions: A naturally occurring hybrid between Achillea clavennae and Achillea tomentosa, King Edward is a compact, mat-forming rock garden yarrow with soft gray-green, ferny foliage and pale primrose-yellow flowers that fade to cream as they age. It stays low and tidy without shearing, making it a long-favored choice for trough gardens, dry stone walls, and the front of a sunny border. Like its parent species, it demands sharp drainage and lean soil; heavy or wet ground causes the crown to rot, especially through humid summers. Deadhead after the main flush to tidy the mat, and lift and divide congested clumps every few years to maintain vigor.

planting.note: Set out divisions or container plants in spring in lean, very well-drained soil in full sun; avoid rich beds, which produce lax, floppy growth.

directions: Raised by the noted English nurseryman Alan Bloom, Anthea is a fernleaf hybrid yarrow related to the popular Moonshine but shorter and denser, with finely cut, silver-gray foliage and flat-topped heads of soft pale lemon-yellow flowers held on sturdy, non-flopping stems from early summer into fall. Its compact habit makes it more self-supporting than many taller yarrow cultivars, and it holds its color and shape well through summer heat. Plant in lean, sharply drained soil in full sun, and avoid rich or consistently moist ground, which shortens its life and encourages crown rot in humid regions. Deadhead spent flower clusters to extend bloom, and divide clumps every two to three years to keep them vigorous.

common_name: Fanal Yarrow (The Beacon, Classic Brilliant Red Yarrow)

planting.note: Set out divisions or container plants in spring in lean, very well-drained soil in full sun.

directions: One of the oldest and most widely grown red-flowered yarrows, Fanal (sold in English-speaking markets as The Beacon) produces flat clusters of brilliant scarlet-red flowers with small gold centers, fading gracefully to salmon and buff tones as they age over a long early-summer to fall bloom season. Plant in lean, fast-draining soil in full sun; rich or wet soil produces weak, floppy stems and shortens the plant's lifespan, particularly in humid climates. Deadhead regularly to prolong flowering and prevent unwanted seedlings, since open-pollinated seedlings will not come true to the parent's vivid color. Divide congested clumps every two to three years in spring to renew vigor, and expect increased flopping and color fading in intense summer heat.
